papers.full_text: SummaryThis Research Topic brings together 22 contributions that showcase the breadth of mathematical and computational tools now used to understand and respond to infectious disease threats. Spanning mechanistic modeling, statistical forecasting, machine learning, stochastic optimization, computational fluid dynamics, and burden analysis, the Research Topic addresses diseases ranging from COVID-19 and influenza to measles, mumps, and dengue. Contributions cluster around three central themes: extracting robust, decision-relevant forecasts from noisy real-time surveillance data; modeling how interventions, mobility, and connectivity shape transmission dynamics; and linking disease burden to environmental, socioeconomic, and health-system determinants. Together, these papers reinforce a unifying message: no single method suffices for every question, and the right analytical approach must be matched to the decision at hand, the data-generating process, and the practical consequences of getting the inference wrong. IntroductionInfectious diseases spread through a complex mix of factors, including pathogens, hosts, behavior, mobility, environment, health systems, and interventions, all of which interact with each other. Mathematical models and data analysis are essential tools for understanding and scientifically simulating these interactions. These approaches enable researchers to draw robust conclusions from incomplete data, formalize competing hypotheses regarding pathogen transmissions and intervention effects, and integrate diverse sources of evidence to generate forecasts and support evidence-based decision-making. The coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic accelerated the use of these tools on an unprecedented scale, with mathematical models informing decisions regarding lockdowns, vaccine allocations, and healthcare capacity-based planning in near real time. But the pandemic also made clear that good models need clear and evidence-based assumptions, must be tested against real data, should be checked against new data whenever possible, and must be used with an understanding of their uncertainty, not treated as perfect predictions (1–3). The challenge has only grown since: infectious-disease data are increasingly high-dimensional and multimodal, spanning genomic surveillance, mobility traces, wastewater signals, and electronic health records, while the methodological toolkit available to analyze them has expanded just as quickly, from classical compartmental models to machine learning and stochastic optimization.The Research Topic Mathematical Modeling and data analysis in infectious diseases responds to this landscape by bringing together 22 contributions spanning public health, applied mathematics, infectious-disease epidemiology, and microbial sciences. The Research Topic covers a wide range of approaches, such as mechanistic modeling, statistical forecasting, machine learning, stochastic optimization, computational fluid dynamics, and burden analyses, applied across diseases including COVID-19, influenza, measles, mumps, dengue, and other pathogens of public health concern. Its unifying message is simple: no single method suffices for every question. Instead, the choice of method should follow from the decision at hand, the process generating the data, the observations actually available, and the consequences of incorrect inference or prediction. Robust inference and disease forecastingSeveral contributions in this Research Topic address a central challenge in infectious-disease surveillance: extracting stable, decision-relevant predictions from data that evolve in real time. Rojas-Díaz et al. propose a robust calibration framework for delayed compartmental models, employing controlled parameter initialization and time-varying parameters to fit COVID-19 incidence, intensive-care burden, and effective reproduction numbers across Chilean regions. Their work underscores practical identifiability and numerical stability as prerequisites for translating mechanistic models into tools that can be used operationally in public health decision-making.A complementary forecasting stream combines classical time-series methods with nonlinear learning. Xian et al. demonstrate that a SARIMA–k-nearest-neighbor (SARIMA-KNN) hybrid model improves prediction of acute hemorrhagic conjunctivitis in Chongqing, China, relative to its component models and Prophet-based comparators. Cao et al. integrated ARIMA and bidirectional long short-term memory networks through genetic-algorithm weighting, reporting improved COVID-19 forecasts for Japan with external validation in Germany. Alahmadi et al. applied seasonal-trend decomposition together with LightGBM to forecast post-pandemic influenza A in Saudi Arabia, illustrating the value of hybrid approaches when seasonal patterns are disrupted by structural change. Collectively, these studies point to an important direction for surveillance practice: hybrid models can disentangle recurrent linear or seasonal structure from irregular non-linear behavior, but their value depends on prospective evaluation and reporting forecasts alongside calibrated measures of uncertainty (3, 4).The Research Topic also moves beyond single-location time series. One contribution introduces a spatiotemporal graph-learning framework that leverages geographic and origin-destination relationships to capture both contemporaneous neighborhood effects and lagged spatial spillovers in infectious-disease prediction (Liu et al.). Taken together with the forecasting studies above, this work underscores that local incidence is shaped not only by its own history but also by connections to other places, reporting processes, and shifting epidemic regimes. Beyond spatial and temporal structure, several contributions strengthen the statistical foundations needed for infectious-disease data that are non-normal, highly skewed, or operationally heterogeneous. Gharaibeh et al. introduced a two-parameter skewed Loai distribution for positive, right-skewed data and demonstrate its competitive fit to COVID-19 mortality data. At the healthcare-facility scale, Chen and Zhou compared SARIMA, ETS, Prophet, and NNETAR models for forecasting multidrug-resistant organism infection rates, showing that model choice should reflect both forecast accuracy and residual diagnostics rather than point-error measures alone. Disease transmission, interventions, and mobilityMechanistic models offer a principled way to represent intervention timing, human behavior, and disease progression explicitly within the model structure. Babasola et al. formulated a time-delayed model for a potential human outbreak of highly pathogenic avian influenza, explicitly incorporating incubation, vaccine deployment, vaccine-to-protection delays, vaccine acceptance, residual susceptibility, and compliance with non-pharmaceutical interventions. Their simulations illustrate why early deployment and rapid protection are critical, and why non-pharmaceutical interventions remain especially important before vaccine-induced protection takes effect. Building on this theme, Ntaimo et al. developed an integrated chance-constrained stochastic-programming model for optimal COVID-19 vaccination and intervention strategies across multiple municipalities in Gauteng, South Africa. By incorporating uncertainty in contact patterns, household transmission, age-specific susceptibility and infectivity, and multiple vaccine-effectiveness endpoints, their approach makes risk tolerance an explicit part of allocation decisions. This work exemplifies a valuable bridge between epidemic modeling and operations research: the goal is not merely to simulate an outbreak but also to identify feasible actions under uncertainty.Mobility is another recurring mechanism in this Research Topic. Drawing on cases from 294 Chinese cities, high-speed-rail records, migration data, and socioeconomic covariates, Zhang et al. found that rail connectivity was associated with early intercity dissemination of COVID-19 and that the Wuhan lockdown and transport suspensions disrupted this pathway. The importance of connectivity is echoed in a different setting: an age-structured, stochastic model of measles outbreaks in Northern British Columbia. Irvine et al. showed that inter-community mobility and school-based contact can increase outbreak probability and diminish the effectiveness of interventions, while the combined use of post-exposure prophylaxis and active case finding substantially reduces outbreak risk across scenarios.At a finer spatial scale, Chong et al. combined epidemiological analyses of high-rise residences in Singapore with computational fluid-dynamics simulations, identifying elevated risk within vertical building stacks, and showed how wind direction and cross-ventilation can shape plausible aerosol transport pathways. Together, these contributions demonstrate that interventions must be conditioned on the structure of connectivity itself: rail networks, buildings, households, and social contacts each create distinct transmission pathways that call for correspondingly tailored control measures. Saha et al. extended this perspective across successive COVID-19 waves through a model-based hypothesis-testing framework that compares competing evolutionary explanations while estimating changes in transmission, virulence, vaccination, immunity, and contact patterns. Their analysis reinforces that epidemic trajectories emerge from the coupling of pathogen evolution and human response and that the dominant mechanism driving transmission may shift as population immunity and intervention conditions evolve. Environment, disease burden, and surveillanceA substantial group of papers demonstrates both the value and the interpretive challenges of linking disease surveillance with environmental, socioeconomic, and health-system data. He et al. assessed meteorological influences on influenza incidence in Wuxi, while Yao et al. examined environmental determinants of influenza-like illness across cities in Fujian Province between 2015 and 2023. Tao et al. characterized severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome and its meteorological associations in Jiangsu Province. Extending this line of work, Guo et al. applied generalized additive and distributed lag non-linear models to identify non-linear, interacting, and delayed meteorological associations with hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome on China's Jiaodong Peninsula. Hao and Yu take a broader ecological view, using provincial panel models to examine bacillary dysentery in China and link incidence to healthcare capacity, economic development, and forest coverage. Together, these studies show that contextual covariates can strengthen local early warning and risk stratification when lagged, non-linear, and place-specific effects are properly accounted for; they also call for careful interpretation, since ecological and predictive associations do not, on their own, establish causation.The Research Topic also broadens its scope from incidence to population-level burden. Luo et al. used Global Burden of Disease data to quantify trends, geographic inequalities, risk factors, and projected trajectories of childhood infectious encephalitis across Asia. Their results highlight persistent inequities, with lower socio-demographic development associated with higher disease burden, and underscore the continuing need to integrate surveillance, diagnostic capacity, perinatal care, environmental protection, and vaccination.Gong et al. similarly used Global Burden of Disease data, inequality analysis, decomposition, age-period-cohort modeling, and forecasting to characterize the global burden of infectious diseases attributable to drug use. At a more local spatial scale, Hu et al. combined spatial autocorrelation analysis, spatial error models, and Geodetector methods to identify clustered gonorrhea incidence and its interacting sociodemographic, healthcare, and environmental correlates in China. Agrawal et al. synthesized evidence from 47 studies and 61 mumps outbreaks across 21 countries, estimating a pooled attack rate of 14.5% and a pooled complication rate of 10.3%, while documenting substantial heterogeneity by setting, age, and vaccination context. Their meta-analysis underscores the importance of standardized reporting and context-sensitive interpretation in an era of waning immunity and uneven vaccine access. More broadly, burden estimation and evidence synthesis connect model outputs to the equity questions that should guide infectious-disease policy. SummaryThis Research Topic brings together 22 contributions that showcase the breadth of mathematical and computational tools now used to understand and respond to infectious disease threats. Spanning mechanistic modeling, statistical forecasting, machine learning, stochastic optimization, computational fluid dynamics, and burden analysis, the Research Topic addresses diseases ranging from COVID-19 and influenza to measles, mumps, and dengue. Contributions cluster around three central themes: extracting robust, decision-relevant forecasts from noisy real-time surveillance data; modeling how interventions, mobility, and connectivity shape transmission dynamics; and linking disease burden to environmental, socioeconomic, and health-system determinants. Together, these papers reinforce a unifying message: no single method suffices for every question, and the right analytical approach must be matched to the decision at hand, the data-generating process, and the practical consequences of getting the inference wrong. papers.title: Clinical and epidemiological structure of imported infectious diseases in Moscow
papers.abstract: The expansion of international tourism and increasing migration have led to a higher risk of the emergence and spread of various infectious diseases, including those that are not endemic to Russia. Therefore, studying the characteristics of infectious diseases in children and adults returning from international travel is of considerable importance. To analyze the clinical and epidemiological characteristics of imported infectious diseases in children and adults after international travel. Materials and Methods . We conducted a single-center retrospective cohort study at Infectious Clinical Hospital No. 1 of the Moscow Department of Health. Medical records of 2005 adults and 501 children who developed illness during or after international travel and were admitted to the hospital’s isolation ward after returning from abroad between 2009 and 2019 were retrospectively reviewed. Statistical analysis was performed using IBM SPSS Statistics version 26.0. The age of the study participants ranged from 1 month to 86 years. Among hospitalized patients, children 1–3 years accounted for the largest proportion (41.9 %). Children were hospitalized more frequently during the summer (176 cases, 35.1 %; p<0.001) and autumn (139 (27,7; 23,6-31,6), p<0,05), whereas adults were more commonly hospitalized in the winter (496 cases, 24.7 %; p<0.001) and in the spring (526 (26,2; 24,5–28,1), p<0,05). In the epidemiological history, travel to the Republic of Türkiye was most common among children (17.0 %), while travel to the Kingdom of Thailand predominated among adults (24.9 %). Compared with adults, children were more frequently diagnosed with enterovirus infection (37.0 % vs 19.2 %, p<0.001) among infections with a fecal-oral transmission route, and pertussis (1.5 % vs 0.1 %, p<0.05) among infections with an airborne transmission route. Among children, dengue fever was the most frequently diagnosed vector-borne infection (88.9 %). We identified the epidemiological characteristics and etiological structure of imported infectious diseases and demonstrated seasonal, geographic, and nosological differences in infectious diseases among children compared with adults after international travel.

papers.title_zh: 莫斯科输入性传染病临床和流行病学结构
papers.source_body_en: The expansion of international tourism and increasing migration have led to a higher risk of the emergence and spread of various infectious diseases, including those that are not endemic to Russia. Therefore, studying the characteristics of infectious diseases in children and adults returning from international travel is of considerable importance. To analyze the clinical and epidemiological characteristics of imported infectious diseases in children and adults after international travel. Materials and Methods . We conducted a single-center retrospective cohort study at Infectious Clinical Hospital No. 1 of the Moscow Department of Health. Medical records of 2005 adults and 501 children who developed illness during or after international travel and were admitted to the hospital’s isolation ward after returning from abroad between 2009 and 2019 were retrospectively reviewed. Statistical analysis was performed using IBM SPSS Statistics version 26.0. The age of the study participants ranged from 1 month to 86 years. Among hospitalized patients, children 1–3 years accounted for the largest proportion (41.9 %). Children were hospitalized more frequently during the summer (176 cases, 35.1 %; p<0.001) and autumn (139 (27,7; 23,6-31,6), p<0,05), whereas adults were more commonly hospitalized in the winter (496 cases, 24.7 %; p<0.001) and in the spring (526 (26,2; 24,5–28,1), p<0,05). In the epidemiological history, travel to the Republic of Türkiye was most common among children (17.0 %), while travel to the Kingdom of Thailand predominated among adults (24.9 %). Compared with adults, children were more frequently diagnosed with enterovirus infection (37.0 % vs 19.2 %, p<0.001) among infections with a fecal-oral transmission route, and pertussis (1.5 % vs 0.1 %, p<0.05) among infections with an airborne transmission route. Among children, dengue fever was the most frequently diagnosed vector-borne infection (88.9 %). We identified the epidemiological characteristics and etiological structure of imported infectious diseases and demonstrated seasonal, geographic, and nosological differences in infectious diseases among children compared with adults after international travel.

papers.title: Production of a Versatile Pan-DENV NS5 Polyclonal Antibody and Structural Epitope Analysis of Immunogen Performance
papers.abstract: Background: Dengue is a major mosquito-borne viral disease worldwide, with approximately 400 million infections reported annually and no fully effective antiviral treatments available. The non-structural protein NS5 is a promising antiviral target due to its critical role in viral RNA replication and host interactions. Although commercial monoclonal and polyclonal anti-NS5 antibodies are available, none were found to combine broad reactivity against all four dengue virus serotypes with suitability for Western Blot (WB), Immunofluorescence (IF), and Immunoprecipitation (IP) assays. This study aimed to develop and functionally characterize a versatile polyclonal antibody targeting a conserved region of DENV NS5 for immunodetection applications. Methods: Conserved recombinant regions from the methyltransferase (MTase) and RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) domains of DENV2 NS5 were expressed in Escherichia coli and used as immunogens in a murine model. Results: Both recombinant proteins exhibited predicted antigenic potential, but only the anti-NS5-RdRp antibody efficiently recognized native NS5 in infected cells. The resulting antibody detected NS5 from all four dengue serotypes in WB, with lower nonspecific background than a widely used commercial antibody. In addition, it proved effective in IF and IP assays in DENV1- and DENV2-infected cells, enabling co-immuno-precipitation of NS3, a known NS5 interactor. Retrospective structural epitope analyses suggested that the RdRp immunogen contained surface-accessible conformational features more compatible with antibody recognition in the native protein context. Conclusion: These findings identify the anti-NS5-RdRp antibody as a valuable tool for dengue research and illustrate how structural epitope analyses can provide insights into differences in immunogen performance

papers.source_body_en: Background: Dengue is a major mosquito-borne viral disease worldwide, with approximately 400 million infections reported annually and no fully effective antiviral treatments available. The non-structural protein NS5 is a promising antiviral target due to its critical role in viral RNA replication and host interactions. Although commercial monoclonal and polyclonal anti-NS5 antibodies are available, none were found to combine broad reactivity against all four dengue virus serotypes with suitability for Western Blot (WB), Immunofluorescence (IF), and Immunoprecipitation (IP) assays. This study aimed to develop and functionally characterize a versatile polyclonal antibody targeting a conserved region of DENV NS5 for immunodetection applications. Methods: Conserved recombinant regions from the methyltransferase (MTase) and RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) domains of DENV2 NS5 were expressed in Escherichia coli and used as immunogens in a murine model. Results: Both recombinant proteins exhibited predicted antigenic potential, but only the anti-NS5-RdRp antibody efficiently recognized native NS5 in infected cells. The resulting antibody detected NS5 from all four dengue serotypes in WB, with lower nonspecific background than a widely used commercial antibody. In addition, it proved effective in IF and IP assays in DENV1- and DENV2-infected cells, enabling co-immuno-precipitation of NS3, a known NS5 interactor. Retrospective structural epitope analyses suggested that the RdRp immunogen contained surface-accessible conformational features more compatible with antibody recognition in the native protein context. Conclusion: These findings identify the anti-NS5-RdRp antibody as a valuable tool for dengue research and illustrate how structural epitope analyses can provide insights into differences in immunogen performance

papers.full_text: ABSTRACTFlooding can disrupt sanitation, contaminate water sources, and alter patterns of infectious disease; however, causal attribution of an individual febrile illness episode to flood exposure is difficult in retrospective hospital-based data. This study described hospitalized patients with acute febrile illness during a post-flood period in northern Vietnam, exploring associations with adverse short-term outcomes. This multicenter retrospective observational cohort included 237 consecutive patients admitted in Thai Nguyen province from October to November 2025. Demographic, documented environmental, clinical, laboratory, etiologic, and treatment data were obtained from medical records. Severe disease occurred in 8.4% and treatment non-response in 6.8% of patients. At admission, mean high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hs-CRP) was 103.3 ± 98.3 mg/L, procalcitonin (PCT) was 6.7 ± 11.6 ng/mL, AST was 55.6 ± 61.4 U/L, ALT was 42.5 ± 46.2 U/L, and GGT was 79.9 ± 70.7 U/L. Recorded etiologic diagnoses most commonly included Escherichia coli (33.3%), Vibrio cholerae (18.1%), influenza viruses (13.5%), Leptospira species (11.0%), and Streptococcus pneumoniae (11.0%). Ceftriaxone was administered to 61.5% of patients. Separate univariable exploratory analyses associated severe-flood residence, non-clean water use, chronic disease history, hs-CRP > 100 mg/L, PCT > 2 ng/mL, and fever duration ≥ 3 days with adverse outcomes. These findings represent within-cohort associations among patients from flood-affected communities and do not indicate that flooding caused the illness episodes or outcomes. Most patients exhibited favorable short-term outcomes.KEYWORDS: Post-flood period, Acute febrile illness, Environmental exposure, Procalcitonin, C-reactive protein. MATERIALS AND METHODSStudy design and reporting guidelineThis multicenter retrospective observational cohort study described hospitalized patients with acute febrile illness during a post-flood period in Thai Nguyen province, Vietnam, from October to November 2025. The study evaluated demographic characteristics, documented environmental indicators, clinical and admission laboratory findings, recorded etiologic diagnoses, antibiotic utilization, disease severity, and treatment response. Reporting followed the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) guidelines. Supplementary Table S1 provides a complete checklist.Study settingPatients were recruited consecutively from Thai Nguyen Central Hospital, Hospital A, Thai Nguyen, and Thai Nguyen University of Medicine and Pharmacy Hospital. These hospitals provide inpatient care to communities affected by seasonal flooding in northern Vietnam. The study followed a major local flooding event with heterogeneous documented impacts, ranging from temporary water coverage to extensive inundation with disruption of care access and water-sanitation systems. No unaffected comparison group or independent event-level hydrological dataset was available.ParticipantsInclusion criteriaPatients aged ≥ 16 years; admitted with acute febrile illness, defined as a body temperature ≥ 38 °C; residing in an area documented as affected by the recent flood or with documented direct or indirect floodwater contact; and who had the demographic, environmental, clinical, and laboratory variables required for the planned analyses were eligible. These criteria defined a post-flood hospital cohort and did not establish that flooding caused the febrile illness.Exclusion criteriaPatients with incomplete records for the required analytic variables, fever clearly attributable to a non-infectious cause, or readmitted for the same illness episode during the study period were excluded. The final analytic cohort comprised 237 patients. The exact number initially screened, and the number excluded for each reason could not be reconstructed from the de-identified analytic files, which is acknowledged as a limitation.Data sources and variable definitionsData were extracted retrospectively from electronic medical records using a standardized case report form. Variables corresponded to the demographic, environmental, clinical, laboratory, etiologic, and treatment data summarized in Tables 1 to 4 and Figures 1 and 2. No missing values were imputed. Diagnoses were obtained from medical records and were not assigned using a uniform study-specific diagnostic panel; the distribution should not be interpreted as the prevalence of uniformly laboratory-confirmed infections.Figure 2Distribution of antibiotics administered during the index hospitalization among 237 patients with acute febrile illness during the post-flood period. Values presented as percentages; percentages may not sum to 100 due to rounding.Demographic and environmental variablesDemographic variables included sex, age, occupation, and treatment hospital. Age was grouped as < 20, 20-39, 40-59, and ≥ 60 years for descriptive analyses. Environmental indicators were obtained from medical-record documentation rather than independently verified geospatial or hydrological measurements. Residence was categorized as a mild-flood area when records described temporary water coverage without major disruption to care access or to essential services, and as a severely flood-affected area when records described extensive inundation with major disruption or contamination of local water and sanitation systems. Water used during and after flooding was categorized as clean when obtained from treated or protected sources-including piped water, bottled water, or protected wells-and as non-clean when obtained from floodwater, surface water, unprotected wells, visibly contaminated water, or another source documented as unsafe.Clinical variablesClinical variables included maximum body temperature recorded at admission, fever duration before admission, treatment duration, chronic disease history, disease severity, and treatment response. Chronic disease history was defined as a physician-diagnosed condition documented before admission. Recorded conditions included cirrhosis, hyperthyroidism, hypertension, hepatitis B, drug addiction, pneumonia, and diabetes. Fever duration was measured as the number of days from symptom onset to hospital admission.Laboratory variablesAll laboratory values reported in Table 2 represent the first available measurements obtained at hospital admission. Parameters included white blood cell count, neutrophil and lymphocyte percentages, red blood cell count, hemoglobin, platelet count, international normalized ratio, glucose, urea, creatinine, aspartate aminotransferase, alanine aminotransferase, gamma-glutamyl transferase, sodium, potassium, chloride, hs-CRP, and PCT. Testing was ordered according to hospital protocols and the treating physician’s clinical judgment rather than a uniform study-specific diagnostic panel. Depending on the suspected syndrome, specimens included blood, urine, stool, sputum, respiratory samples, and other clinically indicated samples.Bacterial organisms were recorded from culture-based or other routine hospital microbiology results. Respiratory viral infections, including influenza, were recorded when supported by antigen-based or molecular tests documented in the record. Dengue virus, hepatitis A virus, Leptospira species, and Rickettsia species were recorded when supported by serologic, antigen-based, or molecular testing according to local protocols.A recorded etiologic diagnosis was accepted when the treating physician documented an organism as clinically relevant and compatible with the syndrome, specimen source, and clinical course. Since confirmation methods differed by pathogen and hospital and were not consistently coded in the de-identified files, recorded etiologic diagnoses could not be reliably separated into uniformly laboratory-confirmed and clinically assigned categories.Microbiological investigations and antibiotic use Figure 1 descriptively summarizes the recorded etiologic diagnoses for the 237 patients. These categories were obtained from the medical records and should not beinterpreted as prevalence estimates of uniformly laboratory-confirmed infection. Recorded diagnoses included dengue virus, Escherichia coli, Staphylococcus aureus, Leptospira species, Rickettsia species, Streptococcus species, Candida species, Streptococcus pneumoniae, hepatitis A virus, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, influenza viruses, Vibrio cholerae, and Salmonella typhi. Antibiotics administered at any time during the index hospitalization are summarized in Figure 2.OutcomesPrimary outcome: disease severityDisease severity constituted the primary outcome, categorized as mild to moderate or severe. Severe disease was defined by the presence of at least one of the following: requirement for intensive monitoring or intensive care unit admission; hemodynamic instability requiring vasopressor support; organ dysfunction, including acute kidney injury, hepatic dysfunction with an international normalized ratio > 1.5, or respiratory compromise requiring oxygen support; or a documented clinical diagnosis of sepsis or septic shock. All other cases were classified as mild to moderate.Secondary outcome: treatment responseSecondary outcome consisted of treatment response, categorized as response or non-response. Treatment response was defined as clinical improvement with resolution of fever and major symptoms, no requirement for escalation of antimicrobial therapy, and discharge without complications. Non-response was defined as persistent fever beyond 72 hours despite treatment, clinical deterioration, escalation to broader-spectrum antimicrobial therapy, or transfer to an intensive care unit.Bias controlDespite use of consecutive inclusion and a standardized case report form to reduce selection and extraction bias, selection bias remained because eligibility required sufficiently complete records. Environmental classifications depended on medical-record documentation, the cohort had no unaffected comparison group, and diagnostic testing was indication-driven. These features limit causal interpretation and may produce differential etiologic ascertainment.Statistical analysisContinuous variables were summarized using minimum, maximum, mean, and standard deviation values, as appropriate; categorical variables were summarized as frequencies and percentages. Separate univariable logistic regression models examined associations with severe disease and treatment non-response, with odds ratios (ORs), 95% confidence intervals (CIs), and two-sided p-values. full_text_sections.results: RESULTSBaseline characteristicsOur analysis included a total of 237 patients hospitalized with acute febrile illness during the post-flood period. Most patients were male (65.0%) and were aged between 40-59 years (39.2%), followed by 20-39 years (34.2%). Most frequent occupational category was freelance work (28.7%). Most patients were treated at the Thai Nguyen Central Hospital (85.2%).Regarding documented environmental indicators, 157 patients (66.2%) resided in mild-flood areas and 80 (33.8%) in severely flood-affected areas. During flooding, 94 patients (39.7%) were classified as using non-clean water; after flooding, 89 (37.6%) were classified as using non-clean water. Maximum admission temperature was ≥ 39 °C in 120 patients (50.6%). Most participants had no documented chronic disease (93.2%). Overall, 20 cases (8.4%) were classified as severe and 217 (91.6%) as mild to moderate (Table 1).Treatment characteristics and outcomesMean treatment duration was 5.1 ± 3.2 days, and mean fever duration was 2.1 ± 1.9 days. Most patients responded to treatment (93.2%); only 6.8% did not respond (Table 1).Laboratory findingsAt admission, mean white blood cell count was 9.4 ± 4.2 ×109/L. Mean neutrophil percentage was 79.5 ± 15.1%, and mean lymphocyte percentage was 12.1 ± 10.7%. Mean hemoglobin level was 134.5 ± 17.3 g/L, and mean platelet count was 214.7 ± 82.2 ×109/L.All values in Table 2 were measured at hospital admission. Mean hs-CRP was 103.3 ± 98.3 mg/L and mean PCT was 6.7 ± 11.6 ng/mL. Mean AST, ALT, and GGT were 55.6 ± 61.4 U/L, 42.5 ± 46.2 U/L, and 79.9 ± 70.7 U/L, respectively. Mean creatinine was 103.1 ± 65.4 μmol/L and mean INR was 1.2 ± 0.1.Recorded infectious etiologiesRecorded etiologic diagnosis was available for all 237 patients. Escherichia coli accounted for 33.3% of recorded diagnoses, followed by Vibrio cholerae (18.1%), influenza viruses (13.5%), Leptospira species (11.0%), and Streptococcus pneumoniae (11.0%). Figure 1 shows the less frequent categories. Since testing was not standardized and the de-identified files did not consistently distinguish laboratory-confirmed from clinically assigned diagnoses, these percentages are descriptive categories from the medical record and should not be interpreted as pathogen prevalence estimates.Antibiotic utilization patternsCeftriaxone was the most frequently administered antibiotic (61.5%), followed by cefoxitin (8.4%), cefoperazone-sulbactam (5.9%), and cefuroxime (3.0%). Figure 2 shows the distribution of antibiotics administered to patients with acute febrile illness during the post-flood period.Exploratory associations with disease severitySeparate univariable analyses associated severe-flood residence with severe disease (OR 3.792, 95% CI 1.079-13.330; p = 0.027). Non-clean water use during flooding (OR 3.118, 95% CI 1.195-8.137; p = 0.015) and after flooding (OR 2.727, 95% CI 1.069-6.960; p = 0.030), chronic disease history (OR 8.059, 95% CI 2.983-21.771; p = 0.001), hs-CRP > 100 mg/L (OR 3.586, 95% CI 1.399-9.189; p = 0.005), PCT > 2 ng/mL (OR 5.623, 95% CI 2.082-15.187; p = 0.001), and fever duration ≥ 3 days (OR 7.923, 95% CI 3.022-20.773; p = 0.001) also correlated with severe disease. Male sex had an imprecise borderline estimate (OR 3.309, 95% CI 0.941-11.642; p = 0.050), whereas age and body temperature showed no association. full_text_sections.discussion: DISCUSSIONEnvironmental exposure and infectious spectrumWithin this flood-affected cohort, residence in a more severely affected area and documented non-clean water use were associated with adverse short-term outcomes. These internal exposure-gradient comparisons are not flood-versus-no-flood estimates and may reflect differences in comorbidity, healthcare access, illness severity at presentation, or other unmeasured factors. These findings therefore do not indicate that flood exposure caused the outcomes, despite correlating with established pathways by which contaminated water and disrupted sanitation can increase infectious hazards 18 - 21 . The heterogeneous recorded etiologic spectrum included enteric, respiratory, and zoonotic categories. However, test selection depended on clinical judgment, methods varied across hospitals and pathogens, and the records did not consistently distinguish laboratory-confirmed from clinically assigned diagnoses. The distribution presented in Figure 1 should therefore be interpreted as descriptive documentation within this hospital cohort rather than the true prevalence of etiologies after flooding 22 , 23 .Inflammatory biomarkers and disease severityMean PCT was 6.7 ± 11.6 ng/mL; PCT > 2 ng/mL was associated with severe disease and treatment non-response in univariable analyses. This threshold should not be used as a stand-alone diagnostic criterion, and the wide variability and limited event counts require cautious interpretation 24 - 27 . Mean hs-CRP was 103.3 ± 98.3 mg/L; hs-CRP > 100 mg/L was associated with both outcomes. These results are consistent with greater systemic inflammation among patients with worse short-term courses, but they do not suggest that hs-CRP or PCT independently determined progression. Larger prospective studies with prespecified adjustment are needed to evaluate incremental clinical utility 28 , 29 .Gastrointestinal and hepatic involvementMean AST, ALT, and GGT values were above typical reference ranges, suggesting the occurrence of biochemical liver abnormalities in some patients. Several infections represented in the cohort can involve the liver, but the study did not include systematic bilirubin measurements, imaging, adjudicated hepatic diagnoses, or longitudinal hepatic outcomes 30 - 33 .Mean INR was 1.2 ± 0.1, which does not suggest frequent marked coagulopathy at cohort level. As only summary laboratory values were available, the data cannot establish the frequency, cause, or clinical consequences of hepatic involvement 34 .Accordingly, the hepatic findings are descriptive and support routine clinical assessment when indicated, rather than a specific gastroenterological conclusion.Comorbidities and host vulnerabilityDocumented chronic disease was associated with severe disease and non-response in univariable analyses. This is biologically plausible, but sparse cells and the lack of multivariable adjustment mean that the magnitude of association may be influenced by age, baseline frailty, type of infection, or other confounders 35 , 36 .Fever duration and clinical progressionFever duration ≥ 3 days was associated with both outcomes. Prolonged fever may reflect delayed presentation, a more persistent infection, or other clinical differences. The retrospective design cannot distinguish these explanations or establish that earlier treatment would have changed outcomes 37 . Most patients exhibited favorable short-term outcomes. Ceftriaxone was the most frequently recorded antibiotic (61.5%) but indication, timing, microbiological appropriateness, and therapy changes were not evaluated. Its utilization pattern should therefore be interpreted descriptively and not as evidence of comparative effectiveness 38 .Sex differencesMale sex presented a borderline association with severe disease, but the CI included 1.0 and the estimate was based on few events. Possible behavioral or occupational explanations remain speculative and require prospective evaluation 39 .Clinical and public health implicationsThese findings support prospective evaluation of documented exposure indicators and admission biomarkers as components of post-flood triage. Such studies should use standardized exposure measures and diagnostic testing, prespecified multivariable models, and external validation. In the present cohort, water-source documentation and admission laboratory assessment were clinically informative descriptors but not validated prediction tools. At the public-health level, access to drinking water, sanitation, vaccination where appropriate, and vector and rodent control remain established priorities after flooding 40 . These general measures are supported by broader evidence rather than by causal estimates from this cohort.LimitationsThis study has several limitations. Its retrospective hospital-based design and requirement for complete analytic records may have introduced selection bias as the exact number of patients screened and excluded could not be reconstructed. All participants came from flood-affected communities, thus the environmental analyses were internal comparisons without a flood-naive baseline. Exposure classifications were based on medical-record documentation rather than independent objective measurements. Diagnostic testing was indication-driven, heterogeneous, and not uniformly coded as laboratory-confirmed, creating differential ascertainment and limiting the interpretation of Figure 1. Study sample was a fixed-period census without an a priori power calculation. Only 20 severe events and 16 non-response events occurred. As 20 univariable tests were performed without multiplicity correction and no multivariable analysis was undertaken, this study’s estimates may be unstable, confounded, and vulnerable to chance findings. Bilirubin, adjudicated hepatic outcomes, and long-term outcomes were unavailable. Finally, findings from Thai Nguyen may not generalize to settings with different populations, flood characteristics, diagnostic resources, or pathogen profiles.
full_text_sections.conclusion: CONCLUSIONSMost patients hospitalized with acute febrile illness during a post-flood period in northern Vietnam presented favorable short-term outcomes. Documented environmental indicators, chronic comorbidity, prolonged ever, hs-CRP, and PCT showed exploratory univariable associations with adverse outcomes in this cohort. These findings are descriptive and hypothesis-generating; they do not establish flood causation or independent prognostic effects.
full_text_sections.other: INTRODUCTIONFloods can contaminate water supplies, disrupt sanitation and healthcare access, and increase contact with environmental hazards, with important health consequences in low- and middle-income settings 1 - 3 . Acute febrile illness after flooding may include enteric, respiratory, vector-borne, and zoonotic infections 4 , 5 . A key evidence gap is the limited hospital-based description of clinical, laboratory, etiologic, and treatment patterns during post-flood periods in northern Vietnam. Temporal proximity to flooding does not establish causation for an individual illness episode; retrospective cohorts are better suited to describe patterns and generate hypotheses than to estimate a flood-attributable effect.Vietnam is vulnerable to recurrent storms and flooding. During the October-November 2025 study period, hospitals in Thai Nguyen served communities with documented temporary inundation and, in more severely affected areas, disruption of access and contamination of local water and sanitation systems. Quantitative hydrological measures for the event were not available in the medical records 6 - 8 .High-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hs-CRP) and procalcitonin (PCT) are routinely available markers of systemic inflammation and infection severity 9 - 12 . Their role here was not to establish novel prognostic thresholds, but to examine whether routinely recorded markers revealed clinically relevant patterns in this post-flood hospital cohort.Environmental documentation, comorbidity, delayed presentation, and inflammatory response may be interrelated. Accordingly, analyses should distinguish the post-flood context from individual-level causal attribution and treat observed associations as potentially confounded and exploratory 13 - 17 .This study describes demographic, documented environmental, clinical, laboratory, recorded etiologic, and treatment characteristics of patients hospitalized with acute febrile illness during a post-flood period in Thai Nguyen province. Additionally, it explores univariable associations with short-term clinical outcomes. No causal effect or validated prediction model was intended.EthicsGiven the retrospective design and use of anonymized medical records, the requirement for informed consent was waived by the committee. analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to explore associations between post-flood environmental factors and adverse outcomes in patients hospitalized with acute febrile illness, addressing the challenge of attributing individual febrile episodes to flood exposure in retrospective hospital-based data.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A multicenter retrospective observational cohort study was conducted in Thai Nguyen province, Vietnam, from October to November 2025, including 237 consecutive patients admitted with acute febrile illness during a post-flood period. Patients were recruited from Thai Nguyen Central Hospital, Hospital A, and Thai Nguyen University of Medicine and Pharmacy Hospital.
analysis.methods: Baseline demographic and clinical characteristics were extracted retrospectively from electronic medical records using a standardized case report form. Separate univariable logistic regression models examined associations with severe disease and treatment non-response, using odds ratios, 95% confidence intervals, and two-sided p-values. Laboratory values were obtained at hospital admission, and fever duration was measured from symptom onset to admission.
analysis.main_results: Severe disease occurred in 8.4% of patients, and treatment non-response was observed in 6.8%. Exploratory univariable associations showed significant links between treatment non-response and place of residence (OR 1.027, 95% CI 1.027-20.880, p=0.030), water use during flooding (OR 1.228, 95% CI 1.228-10.897, p=0.014), and chronic disease history (OR 2.386, 95% CI 2.386-20.747, p=0.001).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted these findings as within-cohort associations rather than causal links between flooding and febrile illness, emphasizing the exploratory nature of the results and the need for further investigation.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings may inform surveillance and risk assessment strategies in flood-affected communities, highlighting potential environmental and clinical factors associated with severe disease and treatment non-response in acute febrile illness.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The analyses were hypothesis-generating and vulnerable to sparse-data instability and confounding, with no adjustment for multiple comparisons. The evidence is moderate due to the exploratory nature and lack of definitive causal conclusions.

analysis.summary_en: This multicenter retrospective observational cohort study investigated associations between post-flood environmental factors and adverse outcomes in patients hospitalized with acute febrile illness in northern Vietnam from October to November 2025. The study included 237 patients and explored factors such as place of residence, water use during and after flooding, and chronic disease history. Results showed that 8.4% of patients experienced severe disease, and 6.8% had treatment non-response. papers.full_text: Interleukin-6 (IL-6) is a pleiotropic cytokine that coordinates innate and adaptive immunity and maintains tissue homeostasis during infection and inflammation. Although transient IL-6 production is essential for host defense, dysregulated or sustained IL-6 activity contributes to immunopathology across infectious and inflammatory diseases. Dengue virus (DENV) infection provides an important context in which this balance may become disrupted. Elevated circulating IL-6 levels are associated with endothelial dysfunction, vascular leakage, coagulopathy, and severe dengue; however, the mechanisms regulating IL-6 bioavailability, signaling duration, and resolution remain incompletely understood. Genetic variation within IL6 and IL6R may influence distinct but interconnected layers of IL-6 regulation. The intronic IL6 rs2069843 and promoter rs1800795 variants have been associated with dengue susceptibility and severity in some populations and proposed to influence IL-6 expression, although their effects are not consistently replicated. In contrast, the functional IL6R rs2228145 (Asp358Ala; also known as rs8192284) variant enhances shedding of membrane-bound IL-6R and increases circulating soluble IL-6R (sIL-6R), thereby altering the extracellular context of IL-6 signaling. Importantly, increased sIL-6R may either facilitate IL-6 trans-signaling or contribute to extracellular buffering depending on the availability of soluble gp130 (sgp130). Experimental evidence for a dendritic cell-derived sIL-6R buffering system provides a physiological framework for understanding this regulation during acute viral infection. In this review, we integrate evidence from human genetics, cytokine biology, receptor signaling, and dengue immunopathogenesis to propose a unified, hypothesis-driven framework of IL-6 regulation. We conceptualize IL6 variants as potential modifiers of IL-6 production, whereas IL6R rs2228145 may modify soluble receptor buffering capacity and the extracellular distribution of IL-6. We further hypothesize that the dynamic balance among IL-6 production, sIL-6R availability, and sgp130-mediated neutralization, together with receptor abundance and ligand-receptor kinetics, may determine the intensity and duration of IL-6 activity more effectively than circulating IL-6 concentration alone. This framework provides experimentally testable hypotheses for understanding inter-individual variation in IL-6 homeostasis and dengue disease progression and may inform future biomarker development and precision immunomodulatory strategies. ConclusionThe unified IL-6-IL-6R framework provides a sophisticated, multi-layered model that reconciles host genetic variation with the complex realities of viral immunopathology. By demonstrating that acute inflammation is governed by a tightly coordinated system of cytokine production, buffering capacity, and receptor availability, this model moves the field past the limitations of traditional, production-centric analysis. Implementing this framework through targeted multi-analyte biomarkers and genotype-guided precision therapies holds immense promise. Ultimately, it allows clinicians to safely restore immune homeostasis, prevent severe endothelial dysfunction, and significantly improve patient outcomes during acute viral infections. IntroductionImmune homeostasis and the IL-6 signaling axisThe ability of the immune system to rapidly eliminate invading pathogens while limiting collateral tissue damage is a defining feature of effective host defense. This delicate equilibrium, commonly referred to as immune homeostasis, depends on the precise temporal and spatial regulation of inflammatory mediators (1–3). Among these, cytokines act as critical molecular messengers that coordinate communication between innate and adaptive immune cells, initiate antimicrobial responses, promote tissue repair, and orchestrate the resolution of inflammation (4–7). While robust cytokine production is indispensable for controlling infection, excessive or prolonged cytokine signaling can disrupt immune homeostasis, resulting in endothelial injury, vascular dysfunction, coagulopathy, and multi-organ pathology (8–11). Consequently, the magnitude, duration, and resolution of cytokine responses are tightly regulated through multiple complementary mechanisms that collectively preserve host integrity (12–14).Among the pleiotropic cytokines involved in the regulation of inflammation, interleukin-6 (IL-6) occupies a central position at the interface between protective immunity and immunopathology (15–17). Produced by diverse cell types, including dendritic cells, monocytes, macrophages, endothelial cells, fibroblasts, and epithelial cells, IL-6 is rapidly induced following the recognition of pathogen-associated molecular patterns by innate immune receptors. Through activation of the Janus kinase (JAK)-signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 (STAT3) pathway, together with MAPK and PI3K-AKT signaling cascades, IL-6 coordinates acute-phase responses, promotes B cell differentiation, supports T follicular helper cell development, influences T helper cell polarization, and regulates tissue repair (18–21). These diverse functions underscore its indispensable role in antimicrobial immunity, while simultaneously explaining why dysregulated IL-6 signaling contributes to numerous inflammatory, autoimmune, and infectious diseases (15, 22–25).Traditionally, studies investigating IL-6 biology have predominantly focused on the mechanisms governing cytokine production, including transcriptional activation, inflammasome-independent induction, and upstream signaling through pattern-recognition receptors (26–30). Elevated circulating IL-6 concentrations have therefore been widely interpreted as a direct surrogate of inflammatory intensity (23, 31–33). However, increasing evidence indicates that cytokine concentration alone cannot fully explain the biological activity of IL-6 or the marked heterogeneity of clinical outcomes observed among individuals exposed to similar inflammatory stimuli. Instead, the biological effects of IL-6 are increasingly recognized to depend not only on the quantity of cytokine produced but also on its persistence, bioavailability, receptor dynamics, and tissue responsiveness (34–38).Recent progress in cytokine biology has started to change this view. The discovery of a dendritic cell-derived soluble receptor buffering system indicates that circulating IL-6 is actively regulated post-secretion via physiological mechanisms that affect cytokine persistence and receptor availability. This emerging concept raises the possibility that immune homeostasis is determined not solely by cytokine production but also by endogenous buffering processes that modulate the duration and magnitude of downstream signaling (39). Such a framework provides a new lens through which host genetic variation affecting either cytokine production or receptor biology can be interpreted.Dengue virus (DENV) infection offers a compelling clinical model for exploring these mechanisms. Severe dengue is consistently associated with markedly elevated IL-6 concentrations, endothelial activation, vascular leakage, and systemic hyperinflammation, yet substantial inter-individual variability exists in disease severity despite comparable viral exposure (15, 40–49). This observation suggests that host-specific regulatory mechanisms, including inherited variation within the IL-6–IL-6R signaling axis, contribute to determining whether IL-6 responses remain protective or progress toward pathological inflammation. In this review, we propose that genetic variation within IL-6 and IL-6R represents two complementary dimensions of cytokine regulation: IL-6 variants primarily influence the magnitude of IL-6 production, whereas IL-6R variants may modify cytokine persistence and bioavailability through soluble receptor dynamics. Together, these mechanisms form the basis of an integrated model of IL-6 homeostasis that provides a conceptual framework for understanding host susceptibility to severe dengue and, more broadly, the regulation of inflammatory responses during acute viral infection. Such a framework provides a new lens through which host genetic variation affecting either cytokine production or receptor biology can be interpreted.Dengue virus (DENV) infection offers a compelling clinical model for exploring these mechanisms. Severe dengue is consistently associated with markedly elevated IL-6 concentrations, endothelial activation, vascular leakage, and systemic hyperinflammation, yet substantial inter-individual variability exists in disease severity despite comparable viral exposure (15, 40–49). This observation suggests that host-specific regulatory mechanisms, including inherited variation within the IL-6–IL-6R signaling axis, contribute to determining whether IL-6 responses remain protective or progress toward pathological inflammation. In this review, we propose that genetic variation within IL-6 and IL-6R represents two complementary dimensions of cytokine regulation: IL-6 variants primarily influence the magnitude of IL-6 production, whereas IL-6R variants may modify cytokine persistence and bioavailability through soluble receptor dynamics. Together, these mechanisms form the basis of an integrated model of IL-6 homeostasis that provides a conceptual framework for understanding host susceptibility to severe dengue and, more broadly, the regulation of inflammatory responses during acute viral infection. IL-6 is not an antiviral cytokine; it is an immunological coordinator that brings together innate pathogen sensing with adaptive immune activation, tissue repair, and the restoration of homeostasis (22, 23, 50). During acute viral infection, transient IL-6 production is essential for mounting an effective host response by promoting leukocyte recruitment, inducing acute-phase proteins, enhancing antibody production, and supporting T-cell differentiation (4–6). However, failure to appropriately regulate IL-6 signaling transforms this protective mediator into a major driver of immunopathology (9, 10, 17, 40). Consequently, IL-6 exemplifies the fundamental principle that the biological consequences of cytokine signaling depend not only on the initiation of inflammatory responses but also on their magnitude, duration, and timely resolution. Endosomal Toll-like receptors (TLR3, TLR7, and TLR8) detect viral RNA, whereas cytosolic sensors, including RIG-I and MDA5, recognize replicating viral genomes. In contrast to interferons, which primarily restrict viral replication, IL-6 coordinates communication between innate and adaptive immune compartments, thereby shaping the magnitude and quality of subsequent immune responses. Additional activation of the MAPK and PI3K–AKT pathways further regulate cell proliferation, differentiation, metabolism, and survival. Classical IL-6 signaling is generally considered essential for physiological immune responses, tissue regeneration, and acute-phase protein synthesis (13, 53, 54).Figure 1Mechanistic divergence of classic and trans-signaling pathways of interleukin-6 (IL-6) during viral infection.Infographic illustrates pathways of IL-6 signaling during virus infection, comparing classic and trans signaling. Classic signaling occurs in nucleus-based cells via membrane-bound IL-6R, while trans signaling involves soluble IL-6R from dendritic cells. Both activate gp130, then Jak-Stat pathways, leading to upregulation of IL-6 target genes.In contrast, IL-6 trans-signaling expands the spectrum of IL-6-responsive cells. The IL-6/sIL-6R complex subsequently binds membrane gp130 expressed on virtually all nucleated cells, enabling IL-6 signaling in tissues lacking membrane IL-6R expression, particularly vascular endothelial cells. This mechanism substantially broadens the inflammatory reach of IL-6 and has been implicated in chronic inflammation, vascular dysfunction, autoimmune disease, and severe viral infections (14, 17, 55). full_text_sections.abstract: Interleukin-6 (IL-6) is a pleiotropic cytokine that coordinates innate and adaptive immunity and maintains tissue homeostasis during infection and inflammation. Although transient IL-6 production is essential for host defense, dysregulated or sustained IL-6 activity contributes to immunopathology across infectious and inflammatory diseases. Dengue virus (DENV) infection provides an important context in which this balance may become disrupted. Elevated circulating IL-6 levels are associated with endothelial dysfunction, vascular leakage, coagulopathy, and severe dengue; however, the mechanisms regulating IL-6 bioavailability, signaling duration, and resolution remain incompletely understood. Genetic variation within IL6 and IL6R may influence distinct but interconnected layers of IL-6 regulation. The intronic IL6 rs2069843 and promoter rs1800795 variants have been associated with dengue susceptibility and severity in some populations and proposed to influence IL-6 expression, although their effects are not consistently replicated. In contrast, the functional IL6R rs2228145 (Asp358Ala; also known as rs8192284) variant enhances shedding of membrane-bound IL-6R and increases circulating soluble IL-6R (sIL-6R), thereby altering the extracellular context of IL-6 signaling. Importantly, increased sIL-6R may either facilitate IL-6 trans-signaling or contribute to extracellular buffering depending on the availability of soluble gp130 (sgp130). Experimental evidence for a dendritic cell-derived sIL-6R buffering system provides a physiological framework for understanding this regulation during acute viral infection. In this review, we integrate evidence from human genetics, cytokine biology, receptor signaling, and dengue immunopathogenesis to propose a unified, hypothesis-driven framework of IL-6 regulation. We conceptualize IL6 variants as potential modifiers of IL-6 production, whereas IL6R rs2228145 may modify soluble receptor buffering capacity and the extracellular distribution of IL-6. We further hypothesize that the dynamic balance among IL-6 production, sIL-6R availability, and sgp130-mediated neutralization, together with receptor abundance and ligand-receptor kinetics, may determine the intensity and duration of IL-6 activity more effectively than circulating IL-6 concentration alone. This framework provides experimentally testable hypotheses for understanding inter-individual variation in IL-6 homeostasis and dengue disease progression and may inform future biomarker development and precision immunomodulatory strategies.
full_text_sections.conclusion: ConclusionThe unified IL-6-IL-6R framework provides a sophisticated, multi-layered model that reconciles host genetic variation with the complex realities of viral immunopathology. By demonstrating that acute inflammation is governed by a tightly coordinated system of cytokine production, buffering capacity, and receptor availability, this model moves the field past the limitations of traditional, production-centric analysis. Implementing this framework through targeted multi-analyte biomarkers and genotype-guided precision therapies holds immense promise. Ultimately, it allows clinicians to safely restore immune homeostasis, prevent severe endothelial dysfunction, and significantly improve patient outcomes during acute viral infections.
full_text_sections.other: IntroductionImmune homeostasis and the IL-6 signaling axisThe ability of the immune system to rapidly eliminate invading pathogens while limiting collateral tissue damage is a defining feature of effective host defense. This delicate equilibrium, commonly referred to as immune homeostasis, depends on the precise temporal and spatial regulation of inflammatory mediators (1–3). Among these, cytokines act as critical molecular messengers that coordinate communication between innate and adaptive immune cells, initiate antimicrobial responses, promote tissue repair, and orchestrate the resolution of inflammation (4–7). While robust cytokine production is indispensable for controlling infection, excessive or prolonged cytokine signaling can disrupt immune homeostasis, resulting in endothelial injury, vascular dysfunction, coagulopathy, and multi-organ pathology (8–11). Consequently, the magnitude, duration, and resolution of cytokine responses are tightly regulated through multiple complementary mechanisms that collectively preserve host integrity (12–14).Among the pleiotropic cytokines involved in the regulation of inflammation, interleukin-6 (IL-6) occupies a central position at the interface between protective immunity and immunopathology (15–17). Produced by diverse cell types, including dendritic cells, monocytes, macrophages, endothelial cells, fibroblasts, and epithelial cells, IL-6 is rapidly induced following the recognition of pathogen-associated molecular patterns by innate immune receptors. Through activation of the Janus kinase (JAK)-signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 (STAT3) pathway, together with MAPK and PI3K-AKT signaling cascades, IL-6 coordinates acute-phase responses, promotes B cell differentiation, supports T follicular helper cell development, influences T helper cell polarization, and regulates tissue repair (18–21). These diverse functions underscore its indispensable role in antimicrobial immunity, while simultaneously explaining why dysregulated IL-6 signaling contributes to numerous inflammatory, autoimmune, and infectious diseases (15, 22–25).Traditionally, studies investigating IL-6 biology have predominantly focused on the mechanisms governing cytokine production, including transcriptional activation, inflammasome-independent induction, and upstream signaling through pattern-recognition receptors (26–30). Elevated circulating IL-6 concentrations have therefore been widely interpreted as a direct surrogate of inflammatory intensity (23, 31–33). However, increasing evidence indicates that cytokine concentration alone cannot fully explain the biological activity of IL-6 or the marked heterogeneity of clinical outcomes observed among individuals exposed to similar inflammatory stimuli. Instead, the biological effects of IL-6 are increasingly recognized to depend not only on the quantity of cytokine produced but also on its persistence, bioavailability, receptor dynamics, and tissue responsiveness (34–38).Recent progress in cytokine biology has started to change this view. analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to understand how IL-6 and IL-6R interactions regulate immune homeostasis during viral infection, particularly in the context of dengue, where dysregulated IL-6 activity contributes to severe disease outcomes.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This review integrates evidence from human genetics, cytokine biology, receptor signaling, and dengue immunopathogenesis to propose a unified framework for IL-6 regulation during acute viral infection, focusing on dengue virus and its associated disease manifestations.
analysis.methods: The authors synthesized findings from genetic studies, cytokine biology, and receptor signaling mechanisms, including the role of IL6 and IL6R variants, to develop a hypothesis-driven model of IL-6 regulation during dengue infection.
analysis.main_results: The review highlights that increased soluble IL-6R (sIL-6R) may either facilitate IL-6 trans-signaling or contribute to extracellular buffering depending on the availability of soluble gp130 (sgp130).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret that the dynamic balance among IL-6 production, sIL-6R availability, and sgp130-mediated neutralization determines the intensity and duration of IL-6 activity more effectively than circulating IL-6 concentration alone.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: This framework may inform future biomarker development and precision immunomodulatory strategies for managing dengue disease and other acute viral infections with similar inflammatory mechanisms.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is a review and does not present original experimental data, which limits the strength of the evidence. However, it integrates multiple lines of research to propose a novel hypothesis.

analysis.summary_en: This review explores the role of IL-6 and IL-6R in immune homeostasis during dengue infection, emphasizing the need to understand how these factors regulate cytokine activity beyond mere concentration. The authors propose a unified framework that integrates genetic, biological, and immunological evidence to explain the balance between IL-6 production, soluble IL-6R availability, and sgp130-mediated neutralization. They highlight that this dynamic system may better determine the intensity and duration of IL-6 signaling than circulating levels alone. The findings suggest potential applications in developing biomarkers and precision therapies for dengue and other viral infections. However, as a review, the study lacks original experimental data, which limits the strength of the evidence. The framework provides a new perspective on how host genetic variation and receptor biology influence immune responses and disease progression.

papers.summary_zh: 在这篇综述中,我们整合了来自人类遗传学、细胞因子生物学、受体信号传导和登革热免疫发病机制的证据,提出了一个统一的、假设驱动的 IL-6 调控框架。在这篇综述中,我们提出IL-6和IL-6R内的遗传变异代表了细胞因子调节的两个互补维度:IL-6变异主要影响IL-6产生的程度,而IL-6R变异可能通过可溶性受体动力学改变细胞因子的持久性和生物利用度。白介素 6 (IL-6) 是一种多效细胞因子,可协调先天性和适应性免疫,并在感染和炎症期间维持组织稳态。尽管短暂的 IL-6 产生对于 宿主 防御至关重要,但失调或持续的 IL-6 活性有助于传染性和炎症性疾病的免疫病理学。登革病毒 (DENV) 感染提供了一个可能破坏这种平衡的重要背景。循环 IL-6 水平升高与内皮功能障碍、血管渗漏、凝血病和 重症登革热 相关;然而,调节 IL-6 生物利用度、信号传导持续时间和分辨率的机制仍不完全清楚。IL6 和 IL6R 内的遗传变异可能影响 IL-6 调节的不同但相互关联的层面。内含子 IL6 rs2069843 和启动子 rs1800795 变体与某些人群的登革热易感性和严重程度相关,并被认为会影响 IL-6 表达,尽管它们的作用并未得到一致的复制。相比之下,功能性 IL6R rs2228145(Asp358Ala;也称为 rs8192284)变体增强膜结合 IL-6R 的脱落并增加循环可溶性 IL-6R (sIL-6R),从而改变 IL-6 信号传导的细胞外环境。

analysis_zh.research_question_and_background: 该研究旨在了解 IL-6 和 IL-6R 相互作用如何在病毒感染期间调节免疫稳态,特别是在登革热情况下,IL-6 活性失调会导致严重的疾病结果。
analysis_zh.study_design_and_population: 本综述整合了来自人类遗传学、细胞因子生物学、受体信号传导和登革热免疫发病机制的证据,提出了急性病毒感染期间 IL-6 调节的统一框架,重点关注 登革病毒 及其相关疾病表现。
analysis_zh.methods: 作者综合了遗传研究、细胞因子生物学和受体信号传导机制(包括 IL6 和 IL6R 变体的作用)的发现,以开发登革热感染期间 IL-6 调节的假设驱动模型。
analysis_zh.main_results: 该综述强调,可溶性 IL-6R (sIL-6R) 的增加可能会促进 IL-6 反式信号传导或有助于细胞外缓冲,具体取决于可溶性 gp130 (sgp130) 的可用性。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者解释说,IL-6 产生、sIL-6R 可用性和 sgp130 介导的中和之间的动态平衡比单独循环 IL-6 浓度更有效地决定了 IL-6 活性的强度和持续时间。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 该框架可能为未来生物标志物的开发和精确的免疫调节策略提供信息,以管理登革热和具有类似炎症机制的其他急性病毒感染。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究是一项综述,没有提供原始实验数据,这限制了证据的强度。然而,它整合了多个研究领域,提出了一个新颖的假设。
